title: Chart casting from date and place

history.detail:
PASS: QA1 gate 1, Sprint 6, audited at commit c9d602e (committed; working tree carries only
sprint bookkeeping). Sprint file re-read fresh immediately before this verdict,
including the 16 Aug re-scope dropping place and houses, and the corrected
Dependencies note.

VERDICT: PASS.

R8 is the criterion this sprint's own risk register says everything rests on --
"astronomical output is unfalsifiable by inspection, wrong values look exactly like
right ones" -- so I did not settle for confirming the tests pass. I measured how far
the adapter actually sits from the cited reference values, across all 30 assertions:

  worst deviation: Neptune @ 1850-01-01 = 0.296 arcmin
  stated tolerance:                       3.0   arcmin
  every other body:                       0.001 - 0.191 arcmin

A tenfold margin, not a suite scraping past its own threshold. I also checked the
reference values are not this codebase's own output laundered back in as a test,
which would make the whole exercise circular. They aren't:
- Sun @ 2024-03-20T12:00:00Z is given as 0.3680844 degrees. The 2024 March equinox
  was 03:06 UTC that day; nine hours later the Sun should sit ~9h x 0.0411 deg/h =
  ~0.37 deg past 0 Aries. The value is derivable from first principles and it
  matches.
- Spot-checked the 2024 instant against known positions independently of this repo:
  Pluto 1.67 Aquarius, Jupiter 14.96 Taurus, Saturn 12.27 Pisces, Uranus 20.27
  Taurus, Neptune 27.48 Pisces, Mars 28.06 Aquarius. All correct for March 2024.
- The 1850 retrograde flags are physically consistent rather than decorative: Mars
  reads retrograde at an elongation of ~161 degrees, i.e. near opposition, which is
  exactly when Mars retrogrades.
Three centuries, an independent source named with its query parameters, a tolerance
justified in prose against the failure modes it is meant to catch. This is how you
test something you cannot eyeball.

Requirements coverage:
R1 MET. `astronomy-engine` is named in exactly one source file, lib/ephemeris/
  adapter.ts (plus package.json and a README sentence). Callers take PlanetName and
  PlanetPosition, never Astronomy.Body. Grepped the whole tree at c9d602e.
R2 MET. All ten bodies, each carrying eclipticLongitude, sign, degreeInSign and
  retrograde. A test asserts the body list matches PLANET_NAMES exactly at every
  reference instant, so a silently dropped planet fails rather than passing quietly.
R3 MET, verified live rather than by reading. Built the app, started it, requested
  /chart: HTTP 200, no redirect, no session check anywhere in the file. There is no
  auth in this application to check against, which is the point.
R4 MET, and better than the criterion asked. The range is enforced inside
  computePositions, not merely rendered as input min/max attributes -- I confirmed
  live that /chart?date=1600-01-01 returns "Date must be between 1700-01-01 and
  2100-12-31." rather than a plausible wrong chart. The part worth calling out is
  calculationInstantForDate's round-trip check: JS silently rolls 2024-02-30 forward
  to 2024-03-01 rather than rejecting it (I verified this in node -- it really does
  return a valid Date), so a nonexistent calendar date would have produced a
  confident chart for the wrong day. That is precisely R4's "silently mis-cast"
  failure, it is not the obvious reading of the requirement, and it was caught and
  tested. /chart?date=2024-02-30 returns "not a valid calendar date." live.
R5 MET. CALCULATION_HOUR_UTC is a named exported constant with the reasoning above
  it, and the page renders both the resolved instant and the rule: "Positions
  calculated for 2024-03-20T12:00:00.000Z -- every date is evaluated at 12:00 UTC,
  not a specific hour you provide." Confirmed in the served HTML. The sentence
  claims exactly the precision the code has and no more, which is the requirement's
  actual intent.
R6 MET. Grepped lib/ephemeris and app/chart for Date.now, new Date(), Math.random
  and fetch: nothing. Every value in computePositions is a pure function of its
  `date` argument. The two module-level Date constructions are literal range bounds,
  not clock reads.
R7 MET. No house, angle, ascendant or midheaven concept anywhere in app/, lib/, or
  supabase/ -- the only grep hits are the test's own describe name and an unrelated
  Supabase config comment. The R7 test asserts the exact key set of a position
  object rather than merely checking a few fields are absent, so adding a house
  property later fails the test instead of slipping through.
R8 MET. See above.

Verified by execution:
- lint, typecheck, test: all exit 0. 57 tests across 6 files, 39 of them in the
  ephemeris adapter.
- next build exits 0; /chart is a dynamic route as it must be, given it reads
  searchParams.
- End to end against the built app: no date -> form only, 200; a valid date -> the
  ten-row table with the instant stated; out-of-range, nonexistent-calendar-date and
  malformed input each -> a distinct, clear message in a role="alert" paragraph.
  Rendered values match the reference set (Sun 0.37 Aries, Pluto 1.67 Aquarius).

Notes, not conditions:
1. The sprint file contains a factual error, and it is the kind someone acts on
   later. Dependencies says, under "Corrected 16 Aug 2026": "Previews were dropped
   from Sprint 5, so there is no pre-production environment: this sprint's changes go
   from `main` straight to production." Sprint 5 did not drop previews. It dropped
   preview *database isolation* -- previews still deploy on every non-main branch,
   which README's "Preview deployments" section states explicitly and which the
   existing origin/preview-check branch demonstrates. Only main's automatic git
   deploy was disabled. The correction therefore understates the safety net rather
   than overstating it, so nothing in this diff is wrong because of it, but the
   record now misdescribes the deployment posture and the next reader will inherit
   that. Worth fixing in the sprint file.
2. "Past date" appears in the Sprint Objective, in R3, and twice in GroundTruth's
   criteria. The implemented range runs to 2100-12-31, so future dates are accepted.
   No acceptance criterion requires rejecting them -- R4 only requires a stated range
   enforced in code, which is satisfied -- so this passes. But the code and the
   stated intent disagree, and that should be settled deliberately rather than
   discovered when someone casts a chart for 2087.
3. app/chart/page.tsx swallows any non-DateInputError: it is replaced with "Something
   went wrong with that date." and nothing is logged. The calculation path is pure
   and range-checked, so an unexpected throw is unlikely -- which is exactly why you
   would never learn about it. One console.error in that branch and it lands in
   Vercel's logs.
4. isRetrograde takes a forward difference over a full day, so it answers "is this
   body retrograde over the next 24 hours" rather than "at this instant". Within a
   day of a station the flag can disagree with a published ephemeris. The method is
   documented in the code and no requirement demands more precision; a centred
   difference around the instant would tighten it if it ever matters.
5. Nothing links /chart from the homepage. Not a requirement, and README names the
   route -- flagging it only so GroundTruth goes straight there instead of hunting
   for a link that does not exist.
6. The error messages echo the submitted date string back into the page. React
   escapes it, so this is text only, not XSS -- I checked the served HTML and the
   quotes come back as ". Same reflected-text nit I raised in Sprint 3, milder
   here because this page has no credential field.
7. Carried forward from Sprints 4 and 5, untouched by this sprint and still open in
   .github/workflows/ci.yml: the local-stack export step is a pipe under a shell with
   -e but no pipefail, so a failing `supabase status` no longer fails that step
   (`shell: bash` fixes it); and `supabase status -o env` dumps every status variable
   including the local SERVICE_ROLE_KEY into the job environment when only the two
   NEXT_PUBLIC_ ones are needed.

Cleared to ship at c9d602e. Standing note for Pipeman: files under docs/sprints/ are
tracked and the tree is dirty with sprint bookkeeping -- do not fold any of it into
the shipped commit, the tree content is what /sprint-ship compares against this
verdict.

PASS: GroundTruth live test, Sprint 6, commit c9d602eec3606f0977d28cb1d7d8c824614222b9. Environment: https://my-little-racoon.vercel.app/chart, 2026-08-16 ~17:35-17:55Z. Reference source: NASA JPL Horizons API (ssd.jpl.nasa.gov/api/horizons.api), geocentric (CENTER='500@399'), QUANTITIES='31' = "Observer-centered IAU76/80 ecliptic-of-date longitude and latitude" -- the same frame a tropical chart uses. VERDICT: PASS. All three criteria verified. The positions are right, checked against an independent published ephemeris rather than against my own belief about where the planets were. Production is serving the shipped commit: page renders c9d602e. CRITERION 1 -- on production, with no sign-in of any kind, a past date returns planetary positions and the page states the instant used. PASS. - Fetched anonymously with plain curl: no credentials, no cookie jar, no session. HTTP/2 200 and a full ten-body table. There is no auth to bypass -- Sprint 3 was reverted -- and nothing prompted for one. - Zero Set-Cookie headers on the response. Nothing is establishing a session. - The instant is stated on the page, verbatim: "Positions calculated for 2024-03-20T12:00:00.000Z - every date is evaluated at 12:00 UTC, not a specific hour you provide." The second clause matters: it declines to imply a precision the tool does not have, which is what R5 asked for. - Supported range is stated on the page: 1700-01-01 to 2100-12-31. CRITERION 2 -- a known historical date produces positions matching a published source. PASS. This is the sprint's actual proof, so I over-tested it rather than taking one date. FIRST, I AVOIDED THE FIXTURES. The repo's own tests use 1850-01-01, 1950-06-15, 2000-01-01 and 2024-03-20. The date suggested to me for this test was 2024-03-20 -- a fixture date, and therefore the single date most likely to be correct even if the ephemeris path were broken or stubbed. I checked it, and then checked four dates the repository has never seen. 48 body-date comparisons across five dates and three centuries. Every sign correct, every retrograde flag correct, worst longitude error 57.5 arcsec (0.016 deg), which is at the display's own rounding granularity of 0.01 deg. 2024-03-20 (fixture date, all 10 bodies): worst 20.4" e.g. Sun app 0.37 vs JPL 0.3680844; Moon 128.29 vs 128.2881499; Neptune 357.48 vs 357.4743468 1789-07-14 (18th century, 8 bodies -- see reference limit below): worst 18.1" e.g. Sun 112.32 vs 112.3234; Mercury 113.42 vs 113.4150 (retrograde) 1801-09-09 (19th century, all 10 bodies): worst 19.6" e.g. Neptune 227.11 vs 227.1103 (1.0"); Pluto 334.44 vs 334.4354 (retrograde) 2024-04-10 (21st century, all 10 bodies): worst 28.2" e.g. Mercury 23.61 vs 23.6150 (retrograde) 2077-05-03 (21st century, future, all 10 bodies): worst 57.5" worst case is the Moon, 172.33 vs 172.3140 -- the Moon moves ~0.55 deg/hour, so it is the body most sensitive to any small difference in time handling or model, and 57" is still an order of magnitude inside anything that would change a chart reading. REFERENCE LIMIT, NOT AN APP FAILURE: Horizons returns "No ephemeris for target Neptune prior to A.D. 1800-JAN-01" and the same for Pluto prior to 1800-JAN-02. So Neptune and Pluto could not be checked on 1789-07-14. That is my source's coverage boundary, not a gap in the application, and it is why I added 1801-09-09 -- it sits just inside Horizons' coverage and closes both bodies on a pre-modern date. THE RETROGRADE COLUMN IS NOT A STUB. This is the check a static audit cannot make and a single-date live test would have missed: on 2024-03-20 every body reads "No", which is exactly what a hardcoded column would look like. So I derived motion direction independently from Horizons, querying each body at D-1 and D+1 and taking the sign of the unwrapped longitude difference, and tested dates chosen to contain real retrogrades. Seven true retrogrades verified against JPL-derived motion, and every "No" verified as genuinely direct: Mercury and Saturn retrograde on 1789-07-14 Pluto retrograde on 1801-09-09 Mercury retrograde on 2024-04-10 Jupiter, Saturn and Uranus retrograde on 2077-05-03 Zero mismatches in either direction across all 48 comparisons. CRITERION 3 -- an out-of-range date is rejected with a clear message rather than a plausible wrong answer. PASS. Verbatim messages, and in every rejecting case NO positions table was rendered -- there is no wrong answer to mistake for a right one: date=1699-12-31 -> "Date must be between 1700-01-01 and 2100-12-31." date=2101-01-01 -> "Date must be between 1700-01-01 and 2100-12-31." date=2024-02-30 -> "\"2024-02-30\" is not a valid calendar date." date=not-a-date -> "\"not-a-date\" is not a date in YYYY-MM-DD form." date= -> no table, form shown The messages are distinguished by failure mode -- out of range, impossible calendar date, malformed string -- rather than one generic "invalid date", which is more than the criterion asked for. 2024-02-30 is a good case: a well-formed string naming a day that does not exist, and it is caught as its own class. BOUNDARIES ARE INCLUSIVE AND CORRECT: 1700-01-01 and 2100-12-31 both render a full table; 1699-12-31 and 2101-01-01 are both rejected. The stated range is the enforced range, off-by-one in neither direction. ADDITIONAL CHECKS BEYOND THE THREE CRITERIA Reflected input is escaped. The error messages echo the user's input, which is a classic reflected-XSS surface, so I probed it: /chart?date= The raw string
